topic: The BJP IT Cell: how a party's social media team became a political machine, and the accusations against it
method: Web search through a search provider; source pages were not opened from the sandbox, so every quotation is the search engine's summary of the source, marked [summary]. Before scripting, open each source and replace summaries with exact quotations. Statuses follow the studio rules: an allegation is always attributed and paired with the response of the accused where one exists. The Tek Fog investigation was retracted by its publisher and is used only as an example of a collapsed accusation. Studies about online abuse that do not attribute it to the IT cell are never presented as if they do. Gaps: the BJP's own published numbers of IT-cell volunteers; AAP, TMC and other parties' cells; the outcome of the Wire case; the original Washington Post text; written replies from the BJP and Amit Malviya (to be requested).

claims.claim: At a meeting of BJP social media volunteers in Kota, Rajasthan, on 22 September 2018, party president Amit Shah said party workers could make any message go viral, true or false. As an example he described a false message, about Akhilesh Yadav slapping his father, that went viral. He said two WhatsApp groups in the 2017 Uttar Pradesh election had 15 lakh and 17 lakh members, 32 lakh in all. The BJP posted the speech on its own YouTube channel.

contradictions: Some outlets give 31 lakh; the 15 + 17 lakh split is consistent.
claims.notes: Use the BJP's own upload of the speech, and quote the exact Hindi words with their context. Check whether Shah also told workers not to spread false messages; if he did, the film must say so.

claims.claim: In 2024 Rest of World and Princeton's Digital Witness Lab reported that BJP-affiliated administrators ran a network of more than 400 WhatsApp groups in Mandi, Himachal Pradesh, a town of about 26,000 people at the 2011 census. They analysed 20 public groups and found praise for Modi and the BJP, along with fake news, conspiracy theories, attack ads and hate speech. One video reached groups with over 1,700 residents within ten minutes.

contradictions: The 400 is the whole network; only 20 groups were analysed.

claims.claim: A peer-reviewed study (Jakesch, Garimella, Eckles and Naaman, CSCW 2021) joined 600 pro-BJP WhatsApp groups during the 2019 election. It found 75 coordinated campaigns that sent 'trend alerts' and produced hundreds of nationwide Twitter trends.

sources.quote: [summary] an organization, most likely the BJP's social media department, develops the campaign narratives

claims.notes: Say 'the researchers believe'; never 'the IT cell ran it'.

claims.claim: An Oxford Internet Institute study of the 2019 election found that 28% of news links shared on pro-BJP Facebook pages were 'junk news', against 21% on pro-Congress pages. On WhatsApp, 34.5% of the BJP's visual content and 28.5% of Congress's was classed as divisive and conspiratorial.

claims.claim: On 1 April 2019 Facebook removed 687 pages and accounts it linked to the Congress IT cell, for 'coordinated inauthentic behaviour'. It also removed 15 pages, groups and accounts linked to Silver Touch, an Ahmedabad IT firm seen as close to the BJP. One of those pages, 'The India Eye', had 2.6 million followers.

Congress said none of its official pages were removed.
claims.notes: Facebook named the Congress IT cell but did not name the BJP. Silver Touch was reported to be behind the NaMo app, which Amit Malviya denied. Fairness: both sides were hit.

claims.claim: On 2 December 2020 Twitter labelled a post by Amit Malviya 'manipulated media'. It was the first such label on an Indian politician's post. His clip of a policeman swinging a baton at an elderly farmer showed only the swing that missed; a longer video showed two policemen swinging, one after the other. The farmer, Sukhdev Singh, said he had been hit.

It reported that at least 23 'surrogate' or 'ghost' advertisers ran 34,884 ads promoting the BJP, against two such advertisers running 3,130 ads for Congress, and that Facebook's system charged the BJP less for ads than Congress in nine of the ten elections studied. Meta said it applies its policies uniformly.

claims.claim: In January 2022 The Wire published an investigation alleging that BJP supporters used an app called 'Tek Fog' to hijack trends. In October 2022 The Wire withdrew it, along with stories claiming Meta gave Amit Malviya special powers, saying it had been deceived by a member of its own team. Malviya filed a complaint, Delhi Police registered an FIR against The Wire, and the Editors Guild withdrew its earlier statement on Tek Fog.

claims.claim: In September 2024 the Bombay High Court struck down the 2023 IT Rules amendment that would have let a government fact-check unit label online content about the government as fake. The challenge was brought by comedian Kunal Kamra, the Editors Guild of India and the Association of Indian Magazines. The Supreme Court had stayed the unit's notification in March 2024.
